drafts.neutral_framing: Should Garland County treat access to food as shared public infrastructure — connecting and scaling community food-growing (gardens on public land, the farmers market, a gleaning and produce-sharing network, and school and campus gardens) the way it supports parks, the library, and water?
drafts.final_wording: Should Garland County back growing and sharing food together as public infrastructure — connecting the gardens, the farmers market, gleaning, and schools it already has, and scaling them — the way it backs parks, the library, and water?
drafts.final_wording_note: Opened by the platform’s founder during the site’s quiet launch. A neutral framing and this plain wording are both logged per the Idea Shaper ownership rules; the plain version was chosen.
shaping_notes: This is a policy question a county or city body could act on — not a named-individual conduct question and not an active ballot measure. It clears the charter’s bright lines.

Mechanism honesty: a county cannot guarantee anyone’s food, and this question does not claim it can. Unlike a from-scratch county, Garland already has the pieces — an active Master Gardener chapter, two existing community/school gardens, a year-round SNAP/WIC farmers market, and a regional food bank — so the honest ask here is to connect and scale what exists, not to invent it.

The evidence base is cited in full on the /food brief and inside each founding solution, with verification caveats stated in the open (the food-insecurity figure differs slightly by data year — 19.6% for 2022 vs. ~20% for 2023 — and both are shown).
drafts.tier_note: Open as a Tier 0 sentiment poll during the site’s quiet launch: no account, one voice per browser, changeable until close. Per the charter, Tier 0 is displayed but never cited as verified resident opinion — verification tiers arrive with the full voting layer.
drafts.background: About one in five people in Garland County are food insecure — Feeding America’s 2023 estimate is ~20% (Aspire Arkansas), and the CHI St. Vincent 2025 Community Health Needs Assessment cites the 2022 figure at 19.6%, with the child rate at 26.2%. Arkansas is the worst-ranked state in the country for food insecurity. Most food help is emergency help, and that work is essential — nothing here replaces it. This question asks about a second, cheaper, more durable thing: whether the county should back growing and sharing food together as public infrastructure. Garland is not starting from zero — it has an active Master Gardener chapter, a year-round SNAP/WIC farmers market, existing school/community gardens, and a regional food bank moving 100,000+ lbs a month — so the real work is to connect and scale them. The full research, with precedents and honest limits, is in Food as a utility.
drafts.disclosure: This question was opened by the platform’s founder. It is disclosed because the platform names who opens every question.

founding_solutions.title: Open public land for gardens — and connect the ones Hot Springs already has
founding_solutions.summary: Garland already grows food together in places that don’t talk to each other: a student-built community garden at the Hot Springs Welcome Center, a grant-winning school garden at the Hot Springs Child Care Center, and an active Garland County Master Gardener chapter tending the courthouse, Entergy Park, and Garvan. Step one is to network them into one visible program and add more — offering unused public parcels for community gardens through a simple revocable license, the model Newark runs at $1 a year and Baltimore runs for free, so no land is sold. Hot Springs Parks & Rec already keeps pollinator and sculpture gardens on city land, so the precedent for city-supported growing space exists. The know-how is already here and free through the Master Gardeners and the county Extension office. Proven at scale elsewhere: Seattle runs 91 community gardens as a city service since 1973; Brown County, Wisconsin runs 13 through its Extension office. Honest limit: a plot supplements a household’s groceries (a California study estimates ~$435 a season), it does not end anyone’s food insecurity.

citations.label: Garland County Master Gardeners / Extension (horticulture agent Arin Shaffer)
Hot Springs Child Care Center — grant-winning school garden (Arkansas Farm to School)
Seattle P-Patch — 91 city-run community gardens since 1973
Newark Adopt-a-Lot ($1/year) and Baltimore Adopt-A-Lot (free) — revocable garden licenses

founding_solutions.title: Hub it at the farmers market — gleaning, SNAP, and a produce-sharing point
founding_solutions.summary: The Historic Hot Springs Farmers Market already runs year-round and already accepts SNAP and WIC — it is the natural hub. Two moves scale it: plug into the statewide Arkansas Gleaning Project (route market and orchard surplus to pantries — call coordinator Brandon Chapman), and add a community fridge or produce-sharing point for daily give-and-take. Project HOPE Food Bank already moves 100,000+ pounds a month to 70+ partner pantries across the region, so the distribution backbone exists — this connects growers to it. Nearly free; the logistics are already running. Honest limits: community fridges are citizen-led mutual aid, not a government program (the Freedge network counted 150+ US fridges in 2021); and whether the market’s past Double Up Food Bucks SNAP-match is still active should be confirmed and, if not, revived.

citations.label: Historic Hot Springs Farmers Market — year-round, accepts SNAP/WIC (City of Hot Springs)
Arkansas Gleaning Project — 12M+ lb, all 75 counties (Arkansas Hunger Relief Alliance)
Project HOPE Food Bank — 100,000+ lb/month to 70+ partner agencies
Community fridges (Freedge model) — citizen-led mutual aid, 150+ US fridges (2021)

founding_solutions.title: Grow it in the schools and at National Park College
founding_solutions.summary: Garland already has a working model: the Hot Springs Child Care Center runs a raised-bed garden that ~75% of its kids take part in, and it won a 2020–21 Arkansas Garden Grant. Extend that pattern across the school district and to National Park College, whose Helping Hawks pantry is already open to the community (a ready outlet for garden produce, though NPC has no garden yet — an opening). School gardens feed cafeterias and teach kids: Denver’s Garden to Cafeteria put 5,000+ pounds into salad bars at ~250 schools, and USDA’s People’s Garden School Pilot partnered with the University of Arkansas to build school gardens through Extension. The evidence is real but honest about itself — the best systematic review links community gardening to higher fruit-and-vegetable intake while stating plainly that the overall evidence quality is low; we keep that caveat attached.

citations.label: Hot Springs Child Care Center — active school garden, Arkansas Garden Grant awardee
National Park College — Helping Hawks food pantry, open to the community
Denver Garden to Cafeteria — 5,000+ lb into ~250 school salad bars
Hume et al. 2022, BMC Public Health — systematic review (higher F&V intake; “evidence quality overall was low”)

founding_solutions.title: Turn the hospital’s health-needs table into a standing food group
founding_solutions.summary: Garland doesn’t need to build a food policy council from scratch — one already meets in all but name. CHI St. Vincent Hot Springs’ 2025 Community Health Needs Assessment names food insecurity as a priority and convened exactly the right people around it: Project HOPE Food Bank, Arkansas Foodbank, Cooperative Christian Ministries & Clinic, and the Garland County Health Department. The move is to make that group a standing food-access working group that coordinates growers, schools, the market, and the pantries — the cheap, structural piece that keeps the gardens and gleaning from staying one-off projects. Johns Hopkins’ Center for a Livable Future documents that such councils can be housed in an existing body; at least 283 were active across the US as of 2020. The north star — honestly out of a county’s scale, but showing the direction: Belo Horizonte runs a food-as-a-right system at ~2% of its city budget, and Rosario turned vacant land into 2,500 tons of food a year.

citations.label: CHI St. Vincent Hot Springs 2025 Community Health Needs Assessment (names food insecurity a priority; lists the partners)
Johns Hopkins Center for a Livable Future — how to structure a food policy council
CDC — 283 food policy councils active in the US as of 2020
Rosario, Argentina — urban agriculture, 2,500 tons/yr (WRI Prize for Cities, 2021)

founding_solutions.title: Build the engine: a food hub with anchor buyers, so it pays for itself
founding_solutions.summary: Gardens, fridges, and gleaning only ever cost money — so on their own they live and die on grants and volunteers. Garland can put an economic engine underneath them, and it has unusually strong demand to sell into: a food hub (aggregation, cold storage, light processing, delivery) that SELLS local food at market rate to buyers who already pay — Oaklawn’s hotels and restaurants, the two hospitals, National Park College dining, the school district, the tourism restaurant scene — and routes its seconds and surplus to Project HOPE’s pantry network. The selling arm funds the giving arm; grants buy one-time capital (the building, the cooler, the truck), not payroll. It is proven: 91% of US food hubs broke even or better in 2020, institutions spend $130 billion a year on food, and Arkansas’s Medicaid nutrition waiver now opens produce prescriptions as a health-care buyer (the hospital already floated a food-prescription program). Honest limit: food hubs still lean on grants (2025 data) and need a real business operator and three to five years to turn — the slow flywheel, not a quick win. The full cited design is at /engine.

citations.label: Food hubs are businesses that mostly break even — 91% in 2020 (MSU National Food Hub Survey)
$130B/year in US institutional food spending — the anchor demand (Health Care Without Harm)
Arkansas’s Medicaid waiver now covers produce prescriptions — health care as a buyer (KFF)
The honest caveat: hubs remain grant-reliant — grants as catalyst, not payroll (MSU 2025 survey)

founding_solutions.title: Fund it with money already aimed at Garland County
founding_solutions.summary: This does not have to come out of the general fund. The Hot Springs Area Community Foundation already names food insecurity as a funding priority and runs open grant cycles (its fall Giving Tree awards $500–$8,000 to nonprofits, schools, churches, and government agencies). The City of Hot Springs is a federal CDBG entitlement community with its own annual application cycle — a food-access project can qualify. USDA’s Community Food Projects grant funds this work at larger scale (up to $400,000, 1:1 match) through a 501(c)(3) such as Project HOPE Food Bank, Jackson House, or CCMC. Extension and Master Gardener support is already free. Spend this money the durable way — on one-time capital and startup (land prep, a cooler, a truck, first-year coordination that hands off to earned revenue), not on payroll that ends when the grant does (see the engine at /engine). Honest limits: grants are competitive and time-limited and most need a nonprofit applicant and a match — seed money to get a program self-sustaining, not a permanent line. (Note: United Way of the Ouachitas, a longtime local funder, closed in August 2025 — it is not a resource anymore.)
